questions.question: In a patient undergoing cardiac surgery, what specific historical factor explains the onset of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) before the conventional postoperative day 5 threshold, and how does this alter the diagnostic timeline?

How does the serotonin-release assay (SRA) profile of autoimmune HIT (aHIT) distinctively differ from classic HIT regarding platelet activation in the absence of heparin, and why might this lead to an 'indeterminate' laboratory report?

When evaluating severe post-cardiac surgery thrombocytopenia accompanied by a new ischemic stroke, which key laboratory finding helps distinguish autoimmune HIT from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?

Given the presence of an acute cerebral infarction and profound thrombocytopenia (platelets <20×10⁹/L), what is the rationale for selecting argatroban over fondaparinux as the initial parenteral anticoagulant in this case?

Why is high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) considered a critical adjunctive therapy specifically for autoimmune HIT, whereas it holds no role in the management of classic heparin-dependent HIT?

Despite therapeutic anticoagulation with argatroban, this patient demonstrated falling fibrinogen levels, rising D-dimers, and new schistocytes. What does this triad indicate regarding the severity of the underlying hypercoagulable state and the adequacy of direct thrombin inhibition alone?

If switching a patient with suspected HIT from argatroban to fondaparinux, why is it necessary to assess antithrombin levels and potentially administer antithrombin concentrate prior to the first dose?

What is the mechanistic significance of observing only partial inhibition of serotonin release when adding an Fc receptor-blocking monoclonal antibody (IV.3) to patient serum in the context of suspected autoimmune HIT?
